title: Blood by Tube
passage:
Carriers drop out of the wall into a bin, one a minute. Jocelyn Ashvenor, a senior biomedical scientist, holds a spun tube to the window. Above the packed cells the plasma is pink.

“That pink is haemoglobin, from the cells,” she says. “They’ve burst on the way over, and their potassium is out in the plasma, so the number I’d report is higher than the patient’s.” Nothing shows on the ward; the colour comes with the spinning.

Last winter Ashvenor taped an accelerometer into a carrier and sent it round the loop for a week. Between stations the shocks were tiny. “It’s the stop at the far end that does it,” she says. The loop runs at the speed it always has. Two bins are lined with foam, and rejects are down by about half. Blood gases have never gone by tube; a porter walks those down.

Nobody has lined the other bins.

– Cheryl Ludlow

questions.rationale:
Option A is the key, and Ashvenor states it herself. Her test was to tape an accelerometer into a carrier and send it round the loop for a week; what the instrument gave back was that “the shocks were tiny” between stations, with the one event worth naming falling at the journey’s end. She says as much: “It’s the stop at the far end that does it”. The remedy points the same way. The loop was left alone and the landing bins were changed, and it is after that change that “rejects are down by about half”. A restates the finding in different words, putting the damage in the arrival rather than in the distance covered.

Option B tempts because the colour is the vivid thing here, and it is easy to carry it back up the chain to the ward, where the blood was taken. The colour is not available there: “Nothing shows on the ward; the colour comes with the spinning.” Whole blood is red throughout; the pink is visible only after the tube has been spun and the plasma has separated from the cells, which is the state of the tube Ashvenor holds to the window.

Option C takes a true thing about blood gases, that they cannot be left standing, and hangs the wrong conclusion on it, one that tempts because urgent work is exactly what a hospital would want a tube for. Their route is given the other way round: “Blood gases have never gone by tube; a porter walks those down.” The half that is true is what makes the whole of it tempting.

Option D tempts because slowing a conveyance is the obvious cure for cargo that keeps breaking, and a fall in rejects is on the page, so anyone who has registered the fall without registering its cause will supply the likely-sounding reason. One sentence rules it out: “The loop runs at the speed it always has.” The change was to the bins, two of which are now lined with foam.

One direction in the mechanism is worth stating plainly, because it inverts easily. The cells break first, and their contents then pass into the plasma around them, which is why she says “their potassium is out in the plasma” and why the figure she would report comes out too high rather than too low. By the same route the pink is haemoglobin released from the cells, not something present in the tube beforehand.
